findings.committee: Sustainable Future City Council Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Hilton Hotel Loan impairment of £10.5m in 2024-25, with further impairment in 2025-26 as site exchanged for sale
findings.detail: The council lent to a Hilton Hotel development. It impaired the loan by £10.5m in 2024-25 after receiving specialist advice and investigations. The sale is now exchanged and will result in a further impairment in 2025-26 accounts, with MRP charged over 20 years. This is a past-tense issue (the sale is progressing) but signals poor asset management and specialist knowledge gaps.
findings.matters: The Hilton loan is a measure of the council's ability to assess and manage complex assets. The impairment is a loss of capital; the ongoing MRP is a revenue cost. A lender needs to know whether the council has improved its due diligence on future investments.
findings.figures: £10.5m impairment 2024-25; further impairment 2025-26; MRP charged over 20 years from impairment
findings.quote: As the sale of the site is now exchanged the Council will be recognising a further impairment within the 2025/26 accounts, which will result in MRP being charged on the impairment over a 20-year period.

findings.committee: Sustainable Future City Council Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Capital financing pressures of £1.7m driven by interest rates remaining higher than budgeted and reliance on external borrowing
findings.detail: The council forecast lower borrowing costs but they have remained elevated. Interest rates have not fallen as expected (base rate dropped from 4.5% to 3.75% by year-end but PWLB rates remain high). The council is also increasingly reliant on external borrowing because internal balances (reserves and cash) have depleted. This pressure will persist if rates remain elevated.
findings.matters: Interest rate risk is material for a council with £486m of gross debt. If rates remain at current levels or rise further, the council's budget headroom reduces. The council's treasury advisors (MUFG) are monitoring, but external rate movements are beyond council control.
findings.figures: £1.7m net pressure on capital financing; net debt £486m (down £39m from £526m previous year); £20m of new PWLB borrowing in February 2026
findings.quote: £1.7m - higher than budgeted costs associated with capital financing. This is partially as a result of budget assumptions requiring a level of reset to reflect the latest interest rate forecasts, and partially due to the delay in realising capital receipts from asset sales

findings.committee: Sustainable Future City Council Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council applied for Exceptional Financial Support (capitalisation direction) of £5m in 2025-26 and £5.7m in 2026-27 to fund revenue pressures
findings.detail: The council requested permission to treat revenue costs as capital (and thus spread the cost over years via borrowing rather than taking the hit in one year). £4m of the £5m request materialised in 2025-26. The direction is 'agreed in principle' but subject to CIPFA's external financial assurance review. This is a sign of structural budget stress: the council cannot close its budget within conventional revenue rules.
findings.matters: A request for exceptional financial support is a red flag to a lender. It indicates the council views its budget challenge as beyond what normal management can address. The direction is not yet final—it depends on CIPFA sign-off, expected June 2026.
findings.figures: £5m capitalisation direction request for 2025-26 (£4m utilised); £5.7m request for 2026-27; decision expected June 2026
findings.quote: Further to this, the Council has submitted a request for Exceptional Financial Support via a Capitalisation direction for £5m in 2025/26 and £5.7m in 2026/27, to fund extraordinary revenue pressures. At the end of the financial year £4m of the identified pressure materialised, and has been funded by the Capitalisation direction, even though at this point, the direction is agreed in principle.

findings.committee: Sustainable Future City Council Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: General Fund reserve of £10.5m is below the council's own adequacy threshold of £12.1m (5% of budget)
findings.detail: The council increased reserves by 47% in 2025-26 (from £5.4m to £10.5m) through asset sales, grant timing, and the capitalisation direction. However, against a 2026-27 budget of £257m, CIPFA recommends 5% held in reserve: £12.1m. The council is still £1.6m short. The forecast shows it intends to rebuild 'during the year' but this signals a council operating with less financial headroom than is prudent for an authority of this size and complexity.
findings.matters: Reserves below the council's own adequacy threshold are a warning sign. They indicate the council has limited ability to absorb unexpected costs without borrowing or cutting services.
findings.figures: General Fund balance 1 April 2026: £10.5m; CIPFA recommended minimum (5% of £257m budget): £12.1m; shortfall £1.6m
findings.quote: CIPFA recommends that 5% of the net revenue budget should be held in the General Fund, based on the net revenue budget for 2026/27 (£257m) the Council should hold £12.1m. On 1st April 2026 the balance is below this level at £10.5m, but during the year it is intended it will be rebuilt, exceeding the desired level.

findings.committee: Sustainable Future City Council Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Unlawful decisions on property and emergency accommodation recorded in s5a & s114a reports in December 2025 and January 2026
findings.detail: The council issued two statutory reports of the s151 officer and monitoring officer in consecutive months detailing unlawful decisions: the disposal of the John Mansfield Centre in 2020 (the impairment of which had already cost £10.5m), and unlawful payments for emergency accommodation. The council has since established a Property Board, reviewed governance templates, and increased property decision scrutiny. This is a control failure at the heart of financial administration.
findings.matters: S5a and s114a reports are serious. They indicate the council was making decisions that breached law without internal control catching them. A lender needs to understand the depth of the control failure and the confidence in remediation. The Property Board and governance review are necessary but may not be sufficient.
findings.figures: Two statutory reports issued within 6 weeks; John Mansfield Centre impairment £10.5m in 2024-25, further impairment in 2025-26
findings.quote: In December 2025 a joint s5a & s114a Report setting out the unlawful disposal of the John Mansfield Centre (JMC) in 2020, was issued to the executive with a further S5a & s114a Report concerning unlawful payments made in respect of emergency accommodation also being issued in January 2026.

findings.committee: Sustainable Future City Council Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: DSG deficit of £11m requires ongoing borrowing at £0.4m per £10m borrowed, to be 'resolved' by 90% government bailout from April 2028
findings.detail: The schools grant overspent by £7.4m in-year, taking the cumulative deficit to £11m. The council must borrow to cover this, costing approximately £400k per £10m. The government has committed to covering 90% from April 2028 IF the council has an action plan in place. This is a material cost hanging over the budget until then, and dependent on a government commitment that could change.
findings.matters: This is a known, quantified future problem with a proposed government solution. A lender needs to assess the risk of the government changing course, and the cost impact if it does. Until April 2028, the council is carrying the full cost.
findings.figures: £11m cumulative DSG deficit; £7.4m overspend in 2025-26; borrowing cost of £400k per £10m; government to cover 90% of deficit accrued to 31 March 2026 from April 2028
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) has overspent by £7.4m, mainly in relation to the High Needs Block, due to rising demand for Education, Health and Care plans (EHCP's) and special school places. This overspend has resulted in a total £11m deficit at the end of 2025/26... At present the Council must borrow to cover the deficit, incurring substantial interest costs, with every £10m borrowed adding approximately £0.4m of cost to the General Fund.

findings.committee: Sustainable Future City Council Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Children's placements budget structurally broken: high-cost residential placements exceeding expectation despite lower overall numbers
findings.detail: The council budgeted for 458 Children in Care placements and ended with 432—a 6% reduction. However, the mix was wrong: more children than expected are in expensive residential placements, with one at 'exceptionally high' cost. The council has shifted to a 'Family First' model and is increasing foster care (140 to 154), but the immediate financial pressure is £2.0m and the underlying problem (high-cost placements on a growing-demand service) remains unresolved.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this is a one-off or structural. The council is trying prevention and early help, but demand for high-cost residential placements is rising even as headline numbers fall. This is a hard-to-fix problem that will recur.
findings.figures: £2.0m overspend; 432 placements vs 458 budgeted; average cost per placement higher than expected
findings.quote: the Placements budget was built on an assumption there would be an average of 458 Looked after Children. At the end of March there were 432, but the placements composition is not as budgeted, with more children than expected in higher cost residential placements and one in an exceptionally high placement.

findings.committee: Sustainable Future City Council Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Savings plan collapsed to 71% delivery, leaving £6.6m of budgeted reductions unachieved
findings.detail: The council planned ambitious savings but delivered only 71%. The failures span service design (PCHLL transfer paused), enforcement (Civil Penalties and Licensing delayed), procurement (£0.9m unachieved, service under external review), and management structure (£0.7m of £2m target dropped from 2026-27 budget). These were not minor slips—they were material budget assumptions that did not materialise.
findings.matters: Unachieved savings are a leading indicator of either unrealistic planning or execution failures. The breadth here—across procurement, culture, regulatory, and structure—suggests planning discipline rather than a single service failure. The council has now removed several of these targets from 2026-27 budget, admitting they are undeliverable.
findings.figures: £6.6m of £23.4m savings programme unachieved (29%); Culture £1.3m, Housing Standards £1.1m, Procurement £0.9m, Peterborough Ltd £0.8m, Management Structure £0.7m
findings.quote: In total, 71% of the ambitious savings programme was achieved, leaving £6.6m needing to be mitigated as part of the overall outturn position.

findings.committee: Sustainable Future City Council Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Revenue overspend of £2.6m absorbed from General Fund balance, with limited underlying improvement narrative
findings.detail: The council finished the year £2.6m overspent, funded from General Fund reserves. While this represents a £3.3m improvement from the December forecast, the underlying issues persist: demand pressures in children's services, unachieved savings, and income shortfalls. The council describes this as 'a £3.3m improvement' but the primary mitigation was reserve drawdown, not operational fix.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can sustain itself without systematically drawing down reserves. Persistent small overspends funded from reserves are the pattern before a larger crisis.
findings.figures: £2.6m overspend against £202m net revenue budget (1.3%); improved from £5.9m forecast in December 2025
findings.quote: the year-end position was an overspend of £2.6m which is a £3.3m improvement to the £5.9m overspend reported in December and this will be funded from the General Fund balance.

findings.paper_title: 12 Corporate Services report to Audit Committee following Section 5 notice July 2026 - Copy
findings.headline: Rolling contracts masked cumulative spend, allowing thresholds to be exceeded without detection
findings.detail: People Services identified 14 suppliers (£125k) where governance failed because rolling contracts hid cumulative expenditure over multiple years. Training and development courses were assessed for compliance at individual contract level rather than total spend to each provider, causing spend thresholds to be exceeded without triggering proper governance.
findings.matters: This control failure creates a structural blind spot where councils can unintentionally exceed procurement thresholds or accumulate large obligations without competitive processes or proper oversight.
findings.figures: 14 suppliers, £125k in People Services
findings.quote: The underlying cause was primarily the use of rolling contracts and a lack of visibility of cumulative expenditure over a number of years, particularly in relation to training and development courses. This resulted in spend thresholds being assessed at an individual contract level rather than across the total value of services commissioned over time.

findings.paper_title: 12 Corporate Services report to Audit Committee following Section 5 notice July 2026 - Copy
findings.headline: Uncontrolled social care temporary staffing overspend requiring Cabinet approval for extension
findings.detail: A large-scale corporate contract for temporary agency cover has identified an overspend while an extension was being considered. Demand from Children's Services increased significantly since the contract began in October 2023. Council will seek Cabinet approval on 21 July to extend the contract and regularise the overspend.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled agency staffing costs are a classic source of council budget failure; the council is seeking Cabinet ratification after overspending, suggesting spending was not managed within approved limits.
findings.figures: Contract began October 2023; Cabinet decision due 21 July 2026
findings.quote: a further large-scale corporate contract for temporary agency cover identified an overspend while a one-year extension was being considered. The proposed extension and regularisation of spend are now the subject of a Cabinet paper, due to be considered on 21 July

findings.paper_title: 12 Corporate Services report to Audit Committee following Section 5 notice July 2026 - Copy
findings.headline: £309k+ of procurement non-compliance found in £25.5m Corporate Services spend
findings.detail: Review of 2,076 payments identified 31 areas requiring action: People Services £125k (14 suppliers), Operations £95k (5 suppliers), Digital & Customer Access £93k. Root causes: inadequate training on procurement rules, poor contract management, and lack of visibility of cumulative spend over time.
findings.matters: Widespread compliance failures in core corporate functions suggest systemic control weaknesses and increase the risk of future overspends or uncontrolled commitments.
findings.figures: £25,511,312.79 spend; 31 items requiring review or action
findings.quote: A number of themes have emerged from the reviews undertaken within Corporate Services and it is very likely these will be replicated across the other directorates as they progress the reviews.

findings.paper_title: 12 Corporate Services report to Audit Committee following Section 5 notice July 2026 - Copy
findings.headline: Section 5 statutory notice issued for governance and compliance failures requiring council-wide review
findings.detail: On 20 January 2026, the council's Monitoring Officer and Section 151 Officer issued a statutory report requiring all service directors to confirm procurement compliance or provide clear timelines for remediation. This Corporate Services report is the first departmental update on compliance.
findings.matters: Section 5 notices indicate serious governance weaknesses; they signal the council's internal controls over procurement and contract management failed systematically.
findings.figures: Issued 20 January 2026
findings.quote: On 20 January 2026, Cabinet received a report from the Council's Monitoring Officer and Section 151 Officer ('the Statutory report') and agreed to conduct a review into Council wide governance arrangements.

findings.paper_title: 08 Peterborough City Council - Draft Audit Plan May 2026.pdf
findings.headline: Audit will not rebuild assurance over prior-year historical position in 2025/26 due to incomplete 2023/24 and 2024/25 audits
findings.detail: Because auditors could not complete planned procedures for 2023/24 and 2024/25, they will not attempt to rebuild assurance over the historical position (2021/22 onwards) during 2025/26. Instead, they will focus on current-year procedures. This creates a multi-year gap in audited assurance over the council's reserves and cumulative balances. The audit plan states it is "unlikely that we will commence any rebuilding of assurance over the historic position during the 2025/26 audit cycle."
findings.matters: Lack of audited assurance over prior-year balances means the council's opening position for any forward projections is unverified. Lenders cannot rely on historical trends or reserve adequacy.
findings.figures: Unaudited period: 2021/22 through 2024/25 (4 years); backstop risk assessment for opening balances due by 30 June 2026
findings.quote: it is unlikely that we will commence any rebuilding of assurance over the historic position during the 2025/26 audit cycle. In line with our established prioritisation principles, we will focus our audit resources on rebuilding assurance for those bodies where planned audit procedures were completed in 2023/24 and 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: 08 Peterborough City Council - Draft Audit Plan May 2026.pdf
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) £18.9 million: fraud risk retained due to manipulation opportunity and late management responses
findings.detail: The council set aside £18.9 million for MRP in 2024/25, but auditors could not conclude their work because council did not respond to queries timely. MRP is a statutory contribution from revenue to reduce borrowing; auditors have flagged it as fraud risk because the judgemental statutory guidance creates opportunity for manipulation to achieve budget targets. Prior audit in 2020/21 identified and reported an MRP calculation error.
findings.matters: MRP directly affects general fund balance and borrowing capacity. If understated, it overstates available resources and masks true borrowing needs. Repeated audit queries and late responses suggest potential avoidance.
findings.figures: £18.9 million MRP allocation in 2024/25
findings.quote: In 2024/25, the Council set aside £18.9 million for MRP. However, we were unable to conclude our work in 2024/25, as the Council did not respond to our queries in a timely manner. Due to the judgemental nature of the statutory guidance, we consider that there is the opportunity for manipulation of the MRP charge.

findings.paper_title: 08 Peterborough City Council - Draft Audit Plan May 2026.pdf
findings.headline: IFRS 16 leases not implemented in 2024/25 financial statements; identified as significant risk for 2025/26
findings.detail: IFRS 16 was mandatory for local government periods beginning 1 April 2024. Peterborough did not implement this in their 2024/25 draft statements because they had not completed analysis of which leases/assets fell in scope. Auditors flagged inability to audit this standard as a reason for their inability to conclude 2024/25 work and have retained it as significant risk for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Lease accounting can materially affect both liabilities (right-of-use asset lease obligations) and operating costs. Non-implementation suggests further financial statement delays possible.
findings.figures: IFRS 16 implementation deadline: 1 April 2024; not completed as of 2024/25 financial statements
findings.quote: IFRS 16 Leases was applicable in local government for periods beginning 1 April 2024... In 2024/25, the Council did not account for the implementation of IFRS 16 as the Council had not completed their analysis of the leases/assets caught within the scope of this revised accounting standard. We were therefore unable to audit the implementation of IFRS 16 in 2024/25. We have identified this as a significant risk in 2025/26 as the improper implementation of IFRS 16, including the valuation and accounting treatment of leases, could lead to a material misstatement in the financial statements of the Council.

findings.paper_title: 08 Peterborough City Council - Draft Audit Plan May 2026.pdf
findings.headline: Major valuation risks retained: £408 million Other Land and Buildings with new valuer and £71 million specialised asset
findings.detail: Other Land and Buildings now flagged as increased risk. The council has engaged a new valuer for a £71 million Energy from Waste Plant (specialised asset requiring complex valuation). Additionally, disposed assets (particularly schools converted to academy status) have not been timely removed from the Fixed Asset Register in prior years, a weakness that persisted into 2024/25. This means assets the council no longer owns or controls remained on the balance sheet.
findings.matters: The £408 million balance represents 6.8% of total materiality threshold. Valuation errors, use of new valuers, and documented weakness in asset disposal controls create real risk of material balance sheet misstatement.
findings.figures: Other Land and Buildings: £408 million net book value; Energy from Waste Plant: £71 million depreciable value; materiality: £6.0 million
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2025, the Council had a significant Other Land and Buildings balance with a total net book value of £408 million. This balance includes a specialised asset called Energy from Waste Plant with a total depreciable value of £71 million in 2024/25. We have been informed that the Council has engaged a new valuer to undertake the valuation of this specialised asset in 2025/26. Increase in risk designation: the audit findings in prior years indicate a risk relating to existence of Other Land and Buildings due to the untimely removal of disposed assets from the Fixed Asset Register (FAR).

findings.paper_title: 08 Peterborough City Council - Draft Audit Plan May 2026.pdf
findings.headline: Material audit errors in prior year not yet remediated: £199 million pension liability misstatement
findings.detail: In 2024/25, auditors identified a £199 million misstatement in the pension liability valuation due to incorrect application of the asset ceiling methodology under IAS 19. While auditors note management has now agreed work with the actuary on this issue, the fact that such a large error occurred and went undetected indicates serious weakness in financial controls and management review processes.
findings.matters: A £199 million error (3.3% of council's gross expenditure on services) shows the council's financial position can be materially misstated. Lenders rely on accurate pension liability disclosure.
findings.figures: £199 million pension liability audit difference identified in 2024/25
findings.quote: In 2024/25, our audit procedures identified an audit difference of £199 million in relation to an increase in the valuation of Pension Liability. The misstatement was due to the Council incorrectly applying the impact of the asset ceiling methodology to the valuation of the Pension Liability.

findings.paper_title: 08 Peterborough City Council - Draft Audit Plan May 2026.pdf
findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinion and failure to recover despite remediation efforts
findings.detail: The council received a disclaimed audit opinion in 2023/24 when draft statements weren't published until 1 August 2024, preventing completion of audit procedures before the backstop date. In 2024/25, auditors again could not conclude their work due to insufficient evidence and late management responses. The auditors explicitly state management is responsible for leading recovery and must strengthen the control environment, but the evidence shows this has not yet happened.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means lenders cannot rely on audited financial statements for the council's true financial position. This is the most serious audit outcome and indicates fundamental governance and financial control weaknesses.
findings.figures: 2023/24 financial statements published 1 August 2024 (4+ months late); 2024/25 recovery not achieved; prior audit difference: £199 million pension liability misstatement
findings.quote: Management has overall responsibility for leading and sustaining the Council's recovery from a disclaimed audit opinion. This includes ensuring that the financial statements are prepared in accordance with proper practices and supported by complete, accurate and timely audit evidence.

findings.headline: Unresolved demand pressures in social care, homelessness and education with no cost solution identified
findings.detail: The statement identifies demand pressures in social care, homelessness and education as continuing to place significant strain on medium to long-term financial outlook. The Council acknowledges that without addressing underlying drivers of cost and demand, it could face ongoing budgetary risk. It is pursuing a whole-system approach through its Prevention, Independence and Resilience board.
findings.matters: Three major cost-driver services are under uncontrolled demand with no identified solution. These are also the areas most resistant to efficiency savings, making them structural budget pressures.
findings.figures: Ongoing unquantified demand pressure in social care, homelessness, education
findings.quote: Demand pressures in areas such as social care, homelessness and education will continue to place significant strain on the medium to long term financial outlook. Without addressing the underlying drivers of cost and demand, the Council could be exposed to ongoing budgetary risk.

findings.headline: Governance and procurement compliance weaknesses identified in statutory section 5/s114 report
findings.detail: A joint statutory report from the Monitoring Officer and Section 151 Officer issued in January 2026 identified governance and procurement compliance weaknesses following investigation of emergency accommodation procurement arrangements. The Council recognises the importance of maintaining robust governance over procurement and contract management, particularly in urgent circumstances.
findings.matters: A second statutory officer report in one year signals systemic governance and compliance failures. The Council's ability to manage high-pressure procurement decisions lawfully is now in question.
findings.figures: January 2026 statutory report, emergency accommodation procedures
findings.quote: A statutory report issued jointly by the Monitoring Officer and the Section 151 Officer, in January 2026, identified governance and procurement compliance weaknesses.

findings.headline: 2024/25 financial statements received low level audit assurance due to control weaknesses
findings.detail: The External Auditor's Annual Report for 2024/25 identified several weaknesses in the quality of accounts, supporting working papers and audit evidence, resulting in low level of assurance. Significant changes have been made to the finance team and improvement programme implemented, but the statement warns it could be several years before an unqualified audit opinion is achieved.
findings.matters: Weak audit assurance on financial statements means the reliability of reported positions is questionable. The multi-year remediation timeline indicates structural capacity or competence issues within the finance function.
findings.figures: 2024/25 audit, low level of assurance, several years to unqualified opinion
findings.quote: The Auditor's Annual Report concluded that the audit of the 2024/25 financial statements included several weaknesses in the quality of the accounts, supporting working papers and audit evidence, therefore leading to a low level of assurance. Although these actions provide increased assurance over financial reporting and processes, it could be several years before the Council achieves an unqualified audit opinion.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support of £10.7m deployed to maintain reserve adequacy
findings.detail: The Council obtained Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) totalling £10.7m for 2025/26 and 2026/27, using a capitalisation direction to finance revenue costs from capital resources. This was described as a necessary step to ensure the Council's reserve balance remained appropriate. Described explicitly as short-term and one-off.
findings.matters: The Council cannot maintain adequate reserves from its own revenue budget without exceptional government support. This is an indicator of structural financial pressure and reliance on non-recurring measures.
findings.quote: The Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Financial Assurance Review is a mechanism that government has authorised the Council to use to provide financial flexibility for 2025/26 and 2026/27 totalling £10.7m. This was a necessary step to ensure the Council's reserve balance remained at an appropriate level.

findings.headline: John Mansfield Centre disposal ruled unlawful by joint statutory report (December 2025)
findings.detail: A December 2025 joint statutory report from the Monitoring Officer and Section 151 Officer found that the 2020 sale of the John Mansfield Centre was unlawful and undertaken outside delegated authority. The Council has since strengthened asset disposal governance and member oversight, but this is evidence of past control failures in major transactions.
findings.matters: A statutory officer intervention in writing confirms prior misconduct of authority. This demonstrates governance arrangements were insufficient to prevent unlawful acts, raising questions about what other transactions may not have met proper standards.
findings.figures: 2020 sale, January 2026 statutory report issued
findings.quote: A joint statutory report, by the Council's monitoring officer and the Section 151 Officer, published in December 2025, indicated that the disposal and certain associated financial transactions were unlawful and had been undertaken outside of delegated authority.

findings.headline: Year-on-year savings plans of £15-20m only partially delivered, accumulating unmet target
findings.detail: The Council has set £15-20m savings targets annually but only partially delivered them. The statement acknowledges plans were not sufficiently developed, relied on optimistic assumptions and short-term mitigations rather than robust, lasting measures. This cumulative failure has contributed materially to the Council's financial challenges.
findings.matters: Recurring year-on-year savings shortfalls indicate the Council cannot deliver promised financial discipline. Budgetary control reports show ongoing difficulty in full delivery, suggesting the gap is structural, not temporary.
findings.figures: £15-20m annual savings target, partially delivered, not fully delivered annually
findings.quote: Savings plans totalling around £15-20m have been set each year and partially delivered, identifying that the scale and cumulative impact of recurring year-on-year savings have contributed to the Council's financial challenges. The Budget Report highlights the significant annual value of savings assumed and the Budgetary Control Reports show the ongoing difficulty in fully delivering these plans.

findings.headline: £11m SEND deficit growing yearly, with statutory override ending March 2028
findings.detail: Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit has reached £11m and is rising each year due to special educational needs demand. A statutory override currently allows this to be carried as a negative unusable reserve, but the override expires in March 2028. At that point, the Council risks having to fund the remaining deficit from revenue, even with 90% government funding only announced through March 2026.
findings.matters: An uncontrolled demand-driven deficit will consume general reserves and revenue budget capacity. The Government has acknowledged it as a national issue but the Council's exposure remains unresolved.
findings.figures: £11m deficit, rising each year, statutory override ends March 2028, 90% funding only to March 2026
findings.quote: There are significant budgetary pressures due to the rising demand for SEND (special educational needs and disabilities). This has created a Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) Deficit, of £11m, which is rising each year. There is a statutory override in place allowing this to be carried as a negative unusable reserve, but when the override ends in March 2028, there is a risk that the Council may have to fund the remaining deficit.

findings.headline: Loss of experienced staff and institutional knowledge during reorganization
findings.detail: Organizational change is expected to result in loss of experienced staff and institutional knowledge, with increased reliance on temporary resources and competing priorities. This may reduce capacity to maintain effective internal controls and governance discipline.
findings.matters: Experienced finance directors and senior finance staff are critical to council financial management and lender confidence; reorganization risk to staff retention is a material concern.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Organisational change may result in the loss of experienced staff and institutional knowledge. Increased reliance on temporary resources and competing priorities may reduce capacity to maintain effective internal controls and governance discipline.

findings.headline: Financial governance robustness is at risk from transformation costs and competing savings delivery
findings.detail: The paper identifies financial pressures linked to reorganization transformation costs and the delivery of anticipated savings as creating risk to financial governance arrangements. Systems, processes and controls will be in flux while financial management remains critical.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in the council's financial governance during a period when transformation costs may strain reserves and deliver less savings than anticipated.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Financial pressures linked to transformation costs and delivery of anticipated savings may also impact the robustness of financial governance arrangements.

findings.headline: Internal audit resources will be partially diverted to support LGR, reducing planned assurance coverage
findings.detail: The council's internal audit function—which provides independent assurance over governance and controls—will have resources redirected to support the reorganization. The audit opinion explicitly warns this will limit comprehensive coverage of all areas during a period of elevated risk.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on internal audit for independent assurance over financial controls; weakened audit coverage during reorganization means reduced oversight precisely when risk is highest.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Internal Audit resources may be partially redirected to support LGR activity, potentially reducing planned assurance coverage. The evolving control environment and ongoing transformation may also limit the ability to provide a fully comprehensive opinion across all areas.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganization will create gaps in governance accountability and control during transition
findings.detail: Peterborough is undergoing major structural reorganization that will establish shadow authorities and joint programme structures. The audit opinion identifies this as creating ambiguity in roles and responsibilities, with increased risk of gaps in oversight and control. This occurs precisely when assurance is most needed.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that controls remain effective; major reorganization threatens the control environment during the transition period when financial and operational risks are highest.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: During transition, governance arrangements may evolve rapidly, including the establishment of shadow authorities and joint programme structures. This can create ambiguity in roles, responsibilities, and decision-making accountability, increasing the risk of gaps in oversight and control.

findings.paper_title: 10 Head of Internal Audit Opinion Appendix A
findings.headline: External audit inspection overdue: compliance with audit standards not formally verified for several years
findings.detail: Every five years, internal audit teams must undergo external inspection to verify compliance with Global Internal Audit Standards. Peterborough's inspection is overdue. A gap analysis was commissioned instead, but a full external quality assessment (EQA) has been scheduled for 2026.
findings.matters: An overdue external audit inspection means the council cannot formally verify that its internal audit function is meeting professional standards. This undermines confidence in the independence and quality of the assurance it provides.
findings.figures: External inspection overdue (5-year cycle); full EQA to be scheduled during 2026
findings.quote: Every five years audit teams are subject to an external inspection to assess compliance with the GIAS, and where appropriate identify areas for further development. Our external inspection has been overdue...

findings.paper_title: 10 Head of Internal Audit Opinion Appendix A
findings.headline: Decline in audit assurance: no Substantial Assurance opinions this year versus one in prior year
findings.detail: The distribution of audit opinions has shifted downward. In 2025/26, the council received 0 Substantial Assurance opinions and 8 Reasonable Assurance opinions. In 2024/25, there was 1 Substantial and 3 Reasonable. This trend suggests that controls are not being designed or operated as effectively as in prior years.
findings.matters: Declining audit assurance levels indicate the control environment may be deteriorating, which increases business and financial risk. Lenders use audit opinion trends to assess whether a council is gaining or losing control over its operations.
findings.figures: 2025/26: 0 Substantial, 8 Reasonable; 2024/25: 1 Substantial, 3 Reasonable
findings.quote: Assessed the quantity and coverage of internal audit work against the 2025 / 2026 internal audit plan where Internal Audit reviews finalised in 2025/26 show a predominance of 'reasonable' audit opinions

findings.paper_title: 10 Head of Internal Audit Opinion Appendix A
findings.headline: Audit coverage constrained by staffing vacancy and resource limits affecting opinion reliability
findings.detail: The council's Internal Audit team operated at 79% of planned staffing (4.85 FTE delivering audit work out of 6.1 planned), with a Senior Auditor post vacant throughout the year. The Chief Internal Auditor explicitly notes that resourcing issues have continued to affect audit coverage and that greater reliance is being placed on third parties rather than in-house audit work.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on audit opinions as independent assurance of control frameworks. When audit capacity is constrained, the breadth and depth of that assurance is compromised, and opinions may not identify all material weaknesses.
findings.figures: 4.85 FTE of 6.1 FTE (79%); 1 Senior Auditor post vacant
findings.quote: Resourcing remains an important but ongoing issue to address in order to enable greater coverage and reliance on our work rather than that of third parties.

findings.paper_title: 10 Head of Internal Audit Opinion Appendix A
findings.headline: Financial governance weakened: Chief Internal Auditor flags need for improvements in controls and oversight
findings.detail: The Chief Internal Auditor explicitly states that improvements are required in financial governance arrangements, particularly in ensuring consistent application of controls and strengthening financial oversight. This is noted despite an overall reasonable opinion. Two specific areas have been given Limited Assurance: Payment Requisitions and Financial Systems Reconciliations.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council's internal audit function has identified material weaknesses in how the council manages and controls its finances, which raises questions about the reliability of financial reporting and compliance with the council's own procedures.
findings.figures: 2 Limited Assurance audit opinions (Payment Requisitions, Financial Systems Reconciliations); 0 Substantial Assurance opinions in 2025/26 compared to 1 in prior year
findings.quote: However, improvements are required in financial governance arrangements, particularly in ensuring consistent application of controls and strengthening financial oversight.

findings.headline: £2.206m Intangible Assets under Construction incorrectly classified as Property, Plant & Equipment and not corrected by management
findings.detail: The Council classifies 'Intangible Assets under Construction' as Property, Plant and Equipment, contrary to CIPFA Code of Accounting Practice and accounting standards. The value was approximately £2.206m. This difference was not corrected by management.
findings.matters: A £2.2m balance sheet misclassification that management refused to correct indicates inadequate technical accounting knowledge and governance oversight, with implications for reliability of other asset valuations.
findings.figures: £2.206 million incorrectly classified
findings.quote: Our testing identified that the Council classifies their 'Intangible Assets under Construction' as Property, Plant, and Equipment. The CIPFA Code of Accounting Practice and accounting standards state that these additions should be classified as Intangible Assets. The value of these assets under construction was approximately £2.206 million. This difference was not corrected by Management.

findings.headline: OfSTED rated Children's Services as inadequate; Improvement Notice issued with Secretary of State-appointed adviser
findings.detail: Peterborough City Council received an 'inadequate' judgement following an OfSTED Inspection of Children's Services (report published 30 January 2024). An Improvement Notice was issued on 23 April 2025. The Secretary of State appointed an Improvement Adviser who will remain in place until at least 1 April 2026.
findings.matters: A statutory services intervention and ongoing Secretary of State oversight creates reputational risk and operational constraints that may impact the Council's ability to manage its wider services and finances effectively.
findings.figures: Inadequate OfSTED judgment (30 January 2024); Improvement Notice issued 23 April 2025; £3.2m Children's Social Care placement overspend in 2024/25
findings.quote: An Improvement Notice was issued to Peterborough City Council on 23 April 2025 following an 'inadequate' judgement after an OfSTED Inspection of the Council's Children's Services report published on 30 January 2024.

findings.headline: Audit assurance rebuild not expected until 2028/29 at earliest; highly unlikely unqualified opinion by 2026/27
findings.detail: The Council's progress is behind expected timescales for rebuilding assurance. The auditor does not expect an unqualified opinion could be reached until the 2028/29 audit at the earliest, which would be subsequent to any Local Government Reorganisation. This means at least three more years of financial statements with audit qualifications.
findings.matters: Three-year outlook for unqualified accounts means any lender or investor cannot rely on independently verified financial statements during this critical period of the Council's financial recovery.
findings.figures: Disclaimer expected to continue through at least 2026/27; qualified opinion most likely for 2025/26; unqualified not expected before 2028/29
findings.quote: This means it is highly unlikely that audit assurances can be rebuilt to enable an unqualified opinion by 2026/27. We do not expect that an unqualified opinion could be reached until the 2028/29 audit at the earliest, which would be subsequent to any Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: No formal authorization procedure for journals before posting to General Ledger, creating management override risk
findings.detail: The Council does not have any formal procedure for authorisation of journals before they are posted to the General Ledger. While no instances of management override were identified during audit, this represents a significant control weakness in the Council's overall control environment.
findings.matters: Absence of journal authorization controls creates material risk that fraudulent or erroneous transactions could enter the accounts undetected, undermining the reliability of financial reporting.
findings.figures: No formal journal authorization procedure in place
findings.quote: Our audit procedures identified that the Council does not have any formal procedure for the authorisation of journals before they are posted to the General Ledger. Whilst we raised this as a control weakness, we did not identify any instances where this led to management override.

findings.headline: Finance function lacks capacity and expertise; £1.7m payroll and £1.1m pension contributions remain unreconciled
findings.detail: The last full audit prior to current year was of 2020/21 accounts. The intervening three-year period saw significant change in the finance function with loss of corporate knowledge and reliance on interim closedown accountants. Audit identified £1.7m PAYE/National Insurance and £1.1m pension contributions unreconciled as of 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: Material unreconciled amounts in payroll indicate the finance function lacks basic internal controls and the capacity to reliably record Council expenditure, a fundamental requirement for financial stewardship.
findings.figures: £1.7m PAYE/National Insurance unreconciled; £1.1m pension contributions unreconciled (as of 31 March 2025)
findings.quote: We identified £1.7 million of PAYE/National Insurance and £1.1 million of pension contributions which remained unreconciled as of 31 March 2025.

findings.headline: Dedicated School Grant deficit of £3.6m forecast to worsen to £9.7m overspend in 2025/26 due to SEND demand
findings.detail: The Council's DSG balance is a £3.6m deficit as of 31 March 2025, forecast to overspend by a further £9.7m in 2025/26 due to growth in demand for children with Educational Health & Care Plans and increasing complexity of needs. The Council is currently borrowing to fund the DSG deficit at a cost of £0.6m per annum.
findings.matters: SEND deficits represent uncontrollable demand-driven costs that will continue to erode financial sustainability. The statutory override allowing DSG deficits to remain off-balance sheet ends March 2026, which will worsen the Council's reported financial position.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £3.6m (31 March 2025); forecast 2025/26 overspend £9.7m; borrowing cost £0.6m per annum
findings.quote: The Council's DSG balance is £3.6 million deficit as at 31 March 2025 and is forecast to overspend by £9.7 million in 2025/26. At present the Council is having to borrow to fund the DSG deficit at a forecast cost of £0.6 million per annum.

findings.headline: John Mansfield Centre disposal was unlawful, breaching statutory duty to obtain best consideration, with £1m post-disposal costs
findings.detail: The Council's disposal of the John Mansfield Centre was undertaken outside authorised powers and breached the duty under the Local Government Act 1972 to obtain best consideration. The delegated authority framework and controls were insufficient to prevent this unlawful transaction, resulting in subsequent costs of £1m.
findings.matters: A second major governance failure involving unlawful asset disposal demonstrates systematic weaknesses in the Council's delegated authority framework and exposes it to further legal challenges and financial loss.
findings.figures: £1 million post-disposal costs; transaction rendered unlawful
findings.quote: The Council's delegated authority framework and associated controls for the disposal of an asset were insufficient to prevent a financial transaction being undertaken outside authorised powers, resulting in a breach of the duty to obtain best consideration under section 123 of the Local Government Act 1972 and thereby rendering the transaction unlawful.

findings.headline: £17.4m of unlawful expenditure on Emergency Accommodation over 10 years without procurement or contracts
findings.detail: Over a decade (2015-2025), the Council incurred £17.4m of expenditure on Emergency Accommodation without lawful procurement, written contracts, or authorised governance/decision-making. This represents a fundamental and prolonged breakdown in the Council's arrangements for securing value for money.
findings.matters: Unlawful procurement of this scale indicates material weaknesses in the Council's control environment and governance, with risk of further uncontrolled expenditure and legal challenges.
findings.figures: £17.4 million unlawful expenditure (plus VAT) over 10-year period 2015-2025
findings.quote: The Council's financial regulations and application of controls for the procurement of Emergency Accommodation were insufficient to prevent contracts with a total value of £17.4 million (plus VAT) being entered into over a ten-year period between 2015 and 2025, thereby rendering this expenditure as unlawful.

findings.headline: Hilton Hotel loan impaired by £10.5m with asset value collapsed to £4.3m and project unfinished
findings.detail: The Council's £15m 2017 loan to support Hilton Garden Inn construction became problematic when the developer entered administration in October 2023. The Council recognized an Expected Credit Loss impairment of £10.5m as the current asset value is only £4.3m. Outstanding loan amount is around £17m with no resolution path identified.
findings.matters: A £10.5m impairment on a capital investment represents a material loss of public funds and demonstrates the Council's exposure to complex commercial projects it may lack capacity to manage effectively.
findings.figures: Original loan £15m (2017); Expected Credit Loss impairment £10.5m; current asset value £4.3m; outstanding loan amount ~£17m; £1m+ estimated for site restoration
findings.quote: Management's Expected Credit Loss Assessment concluded that the loan receivable should be impaired by £10.5 million, as the current value of the part completed hotel asset or its future economic benefit is only valued at £4.3 million at the 31 March 2025.

findings.headline: Council recorded £5.0m overspend in 2024/25 and forecasts £5.2m overspend in Q1 2025/26 despite setting a balanced budget
findings.detail: The £5.0m overspend was a slight improvement on the Q3 forecast of £5.38m. Key drivers include £3.2m net overspend in Children's Social Care placements, £1.9m impact from high interest rates and asset disposal delays, £1.7m in leisure services, and £1.7m in temporary accommodation. Q1 2025/26 position shows £5.2m forecast overspend.
findings.matters: Persistent overspending despite supposedly balanced budgets demonstrates either weak budget control or structural deficits that cannot be closed through operational measures, both indicators of financial distress.
findings.figures: 2024/25 outturn: £5.0m overspend (improved from £5.38m Q3 forecast); Q1 2025/26: £5.2m forecast overspend; Children's Social Care £3.2m, Capital Financing £1.9m, Leisure £1.7m, Temporary Accommodation £1.7m
findings.quote: The revenue budget is currently forecast to be £5.2 million overspent forecasting forward to year end, reflecting the continued challenging financial position of the Council.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves fell to £25.5m (2024/25) from £48.1m (2023/24), now critically below the £10.6m minimum requirement
findings.detail: Overall reserves decreased by £22.6 million in 2024/25 due to planned investment, funding operational overspends, and inflationary pressures. The Council's minimum reserves policy requires 5% of net revenue expenditure (£10.6m), but current uncommitted reserves are dangerously low with little buffer for shocks.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves indicate the Council is funding ongoing operations from one-time sources and has severely limited capacity to absorb unexpected expenditure or income shortfalls, creating acute refinancing risk.
findings.figures: General Fund and Earmarked Reserves: £48.1m (2023/24) → £25.5m (2024/25); minimum requirement £10.6m; Q1 2025/26 forecast would take balance below £2m if overspend materialises
findings.quote: Usable reserves have diminished sharply, leaving little room for manoeuvre. The Panel warns there is no further scope to use reserves for transformation activities.

findings.headline: Disclaimer of opinion issued on 2024/25 financial statements due to inability to gain sufficient audit assurance
findings.detail: The auditor was unable to obtain sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances. The lack of evidence over these movements and balances, combined with the disclaimer on 2023/24 brought-forward balances, means the auditor could not conclude that the 2024/25 financial statements were free from material and pervasive misstatement.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion is the most severe audit finding and indicates the Council's financial position cannot be reliably established, which is a material concern for any lender assessing creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Disclaimer issued 10 February 2026; lack of assurance over all 2024/25 in-year movements and comparative prior year movements
findings.quote: Although the level of assurance gained has increased, we were not able to obtain sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances... we were unable to conclude that the 2024/25 financial statements were free from material and pervasive misstatement of the financial statements.

findings.headline: Borrowing strategy dependent on interest rates falling, but treasury advisors identify material upside risks
findings.detail: The council is maintaining internal borrowing and deferring long-term external borrowing, betting that PWLB rates will fall to trigger points of 4.5% (current), 4.25% (2026/27), and 4.0% (2027/28). However, section 5.3 notes risks to interest rate forecasts are 'generally to the upsides, especially if inflation remains higher than expected and risk premiums relating to government debt increase.'
findings.matters: If rates do not fall as forecast, the council will be forced to borrow long-term at higher rates than anticipated, materially worsening financing costs and making the internal-borrowing position unsustainable.
findings.figures: Bank Rate forecast 3.75% (Dec 2025) → 3.5% (Q2 2026) → 3.25% (Q4 2026); trigger rates 4.5% to 4.0% over 2026-28
findings.quote: There are risks to the forecasts to the upside, especially if inflation remains higher than expected and risk premiums relating to government debt increase.

findings.headline: Financing costs rising 21% over three years despite forecasts for interest rate cuts
findings.detail: Annual financing costs (debt service) are forecast to grow from £36.2m (2025/26) to £43.7m (2028/29), an increase of £7.5m. This growth occurs even though treasury advisors forecast Bank Rate falling to 3.25% by end-2026. The increase indicates the council will be servicing higher absolute debt levels despite lower rates.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs claim a growing share of the council's budget even before accounting for inflation or service pressures. If interest rates fall more slowly than forecast, financing costs could exceed these projections, squeezing other spending.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing capacity falling sharply as reserves are drawn down to fund budgeted expenditure
findings.detail: The council is depleting its reserves and cash balances to fund spending, reducing internal borrowing from £90m (2025/26) to £40m (2028/29)—a 56% decline in three years. This forces increasing reliance on external borrowing even as the underlying Capital Financing Requirement itself falls, indicating the council cannot sustain expenditure from revenue.
findings.matters: For a lender, declining reserves signal a worsening structural position: the council is running through cash buffers and will need sustained access to external debt markets to close the gap. A lender would want to understand why reserves are being consumed.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing 2025/26 £90.0m → 2026/27 £60.0m → 2028/29 £40.0m; External Borrowing rising from £478.9m (Dec 2025 actual) to £574.2m (2028/29 forecast)
findings.quote: the capacity to use internal borrowing is expected to fall as reserves, balances and grants, currently set aside, are utilised over the next three years to fund budgeted expenditure.

findings.paper_title: (a) Appendix D- Reserves Strategy & Policy 2026-27, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will require significant unquantified resources, with only a small portion committed to date
findings.detail: The council recognises that LGR 'will need significant resources across the region' and states 'as only a small portion has been committed to date, the aim is to increase this reserve to ensure adequate funding'. The Innovation/LGR reserve is available to support LGR costs alongside transformation spending.
findings.matters: Unquantified but acknowledged major costs for LGR represent a significant future draw on reserves; underfunding at the outset suggests potential for further emergency funding calls.
findings.figures: 'Only a small portion' committed; reserve replenished from underspends after General Fund target achieved
findings.quote: It is also recognised that Local Government Reorganisation will need significant resources across the region. As only a small portion has been committed to date, the aim is to increase this reserve to ensure adequate funding.

findings.paper_title: (a) Appendix D- Reserves Strategy & Policy 2026-27, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Business rates changes effective April 2026 create significant forecast uncertainty requiring dedicated risk reserve
findings.detail: Upcoming national changes to business rates from 1 April 2026 have created sufficient forecast uncertainty that the council is maintaining a 'Local Tax Income Risk Reserve' specifically to manage the risks and uncertainties from these changes.
findings.matters: Business rates are a material income source; admitted inability to forecast reliably post-April 2026 suggests the council cannot confidently project income for remainder of financial year.
findings.figures: Changes effective 1 April 2026; within current financial year
findings.quote: Due to upcoming national changes to business rates from 1 April 2026, forecasts remain uncertain.

findings.paper_title: (a) Appendix D- Reserves Strategy & Policy 2026-27, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: External legal costs are placing significant budget pressure and required creation of new Legal and Appeals Reserve
findings.detail: The council has established a new 'Legal and Appeals Reserve' specifically because external legal fees are 'placing significant pressure on the budget, especially in complex cases that address both current and historical matters', indicating ongoing complex litigation creating unbudgeted costs.
findings.matters: Ongoing litigation costs are a sign of underlying governance or operational issues; unplanned legal expenditure indicates budget forecasting difficulties and potential for further surprises.
findings.figures: New reserve created; amount not quantified in strategy
findings.quote: External legal fees are placing significant pressure on the budget, especially in complex cases that address both current and historical matters.

findings.paper_title: (a) Appendix D- Reserves Strategy & Policy 2026-27, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Contingent DSG deficit liability could force reserve depletion or require capitalisation direction if government does not assume SEND costs
findings.detail: The government has announced intent to assume full financial responsibility for SEND provision from April 2028, but 'there remains considerable uncertainty regarding the management of deficits accrued prior to this date'. If this responsibility is not taken over, the new LGR authority will be required to address accumulated deficits. The paper explicitly states this 'may lead to depletion of reserves or necessitate a capitalisation direction'.
findings.matters: A materialised contingent liability of unknown magnitude could force emergency reserve drawdown or require central government bailout intervention, both indicators of financial distress.
findings.figures: Deadline: 31 March 2028; deficits prior to April 2028 in scope; amount unquantified
findings.quote: This scenario may lead to depletion of reserves or necessitate a capitalisation direction.

findings.paper_title: (a) Appendix D- Reserves Strategy & Policy 2026-27, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Council's financial resilience will remain very low until 2027/28 despite a reserve recovery plan beginning in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has not been able to maintain its general fund reserve at the recommended 5% of Net Revenue Expenditure (£12.9m) due to ongoing financial pressures. Reserves have been drawn down faster than replenished, eroding financial resilience. While a three-year recovery plan begins in 2026/27, the council explicitly states it will still face 'very low financial resilience' until 2027/28.
findings.matters: Low reserves indicate financial fragility and vulnerability to unexpected shocks, demand pressures, or emergencies, directly affecting creditworthiness and operational flexibility.
findings.figures: £12.9m (5% of NRE target); three-year recovery plan; low resilience persists until 2027/28
findings.quote: Although a plan to rebuild reserves begins in 2026/27, the Council will still face very low financial resilience until 2027/28.

findings.headline: Resource and capacity risk from restructuring and labour market constraints during major transformation
findings.detail: Resource and Capacity risk is Amber. Restructuring to reduce staff numbers and the reduced availability of skilled workers will potentially impact the council's ability to deliver services and change programmes critical to the financial position, especially with LGR on the horizon.
findings.matters: Inability to execute the savings and transformation programmes underpinning the MTFS would mean the overspend and reserve problems persist or worsen.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: The long-term impact of restructuring to reduce staff numbers and make savings, and the reduced availability of skilled workers, will potentially impact on the Council's ability to deliver services and change programmes, critical to the Councils financial position.

findings.headline: NHS Integration (ICS transition April 2026) may transfer costs from NHS to council budgets
findings.detail: NHS integration is Amber. The shift to Integrated Care Systems on 1 April 2026 risks transferring costs from NHS to council budgets. The council is also pursuing recovery of outstanding balances due from the ICB as at 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: Unexpected cost transfers would exacerbate the current overspend and erode reserves further; unrecovered ICB debts directly reduce council cash.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Key challenges include the possibility of increased financial pressures as costs may be transferred from NHS to council budgets.

findings.headline: Income collection risk particularly from NNDR on retail, hospitality and leisure following relief removal
findings.detail: Income collection is Amber. The council faces non-collection risk on local taxation as businesses and households are affected by cost of living. The removal of Retail, Hospitality and Leisure NNDR relief creates an additional headwind.
findings.matters: With reserves depleted, any shortfall in tax income directly impacts cash flow. The NNDR relief removal specifically targets sectors already under pressure, increasing default risk.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: There is a risk associated with the non-collection of income, particularly in local taxation where businesses and households are affected by the cost of living and changes in legislation around NNDR, specifically those businesses adversely effected by the removal of the Retail, Hospitality and Leisure relief.

findings.headline: Interest rate risk on £61m of maturing debt in refinancing environment
findings.detail: Interest rate risk is Amber. The council faces £61m of maturing debt requiring refinancing, and new borrowing needs. Rising or volatile interest rates could increase debt servicing costs. The ability to internally borrow (use cash balances) is reduced.
findings.matters: With high existing debt and limited cash buffers, interest rate movements directly impact the council's ability to service debt; refinancing at higher rates compounds the overspend and reserve problems.
findings.figures: £61m maturing debt
findings.quote: This could impact the Council's refinancing of £61m maturing debt, new borrowing, and investment returns.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates unquantifiable risk with potential adverse effect on financial position
findings.detail: LGR is rated Red. The council cannot yet fully quantify costs and benefits, but there is explicit risk that these could have an adverse effect on the overall financial position. There is also risk that decisions made now (asset disposal, reserve use, major contracts) could constrain the new authority.
findings.matters: A red-rated risk with unquantifiable impact is a material governance problem; it creates uncertainty around the council's actual financial trajectory and prevents reliable medium-term planning.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: Currently, it is not possible to fully quantify the costs and benefits, but there is a resulting risk that these could have an adverse effect on the overall financial position for the Council or the new authority.

findings.headline: DSG deficit now recorded as negative reserve and requiring additional borrowing
findings.detail: Rising demand on SEND services has created a DSG deficit that is now shown as a negative reserve. This forces borrowing to fund it, placing additional strain on the general fund. Government plans to fully fund SEND from April 2028 but uncertainty remains about how existing deficits will be handled.
findings.matters: A negative reserve is a critical indicator; additional borrowing to cover it increases debt servicing costs and creates ongoing uncertainty if the government changes its April 2028 plan.
findings.figures: DSG deficit shown as negative reserve (amount not specified in this section)
findings.quote: The Council faces major financial pressures due to increased demands on SEND services causing a DSG deficit, that is now shown as a negative reserve. Funding the deficit requires borrowing, further straining the general fund.

findings.headline: Current £7m in-year overspend with low reserves and high borrowing
findings.detail: The council reported a £7m overspend as of November 2025. Reserves remain low and debt stands at £0.5bn. Overall Financial Resilience is rated Amber, improving only over the life of the MTFS, with a reset, rebuild and redesign approach being implemented.
findings.matters: An active overspend mid-year signals cash management problems and the weakened reserve position means limited buffer for unexpected costs.
findings.figures: £7m overspend (November 2025), £0.5bn borrowing, low reserves
findings.quote: In year overspend of £7m reported as of November 2025. Reserves balances remain low. Debt (borrowing) remains high at £0.5bn

findings.paper_title: (a) Appendix F - PCC - Capital Strategy 2026-2029, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: £20 million leisure development funded by Department of Business and Trade grant commitment
findings.detail: The council is committing to a major new leisure facility (Peterborough Leisure development) with £20m secured grant. Expenditure is phased £1.1m (2025/26), £10m (2026/27), £18m (2027/28), £8m (2028/29). While grant-funded, this represents major capital deployment and asset lifecycle commitments.
findings.matters: This is a large discretionary capital commitment that will create future operating and maintenance costs. New leisure facilities typically require subsidy from revenue budgets for operations, competing with core services.
findings.figures: £20 million secured grant; spend profile: £1.1m, £10m, £18m, £8m across 2025/26 to 2028/29
findings.quote: Our goal is to invest the secured £20 million from the Department of Business and Trade into a community asset that will improve health, wellbeing, living standards, and life expectancy.

findings.paper_title: (a) Appendix F - PCC - Capital Strategy 2026-2029, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: SEND specialist provision gap of 150 unfunded placements driving high-cost out-of-county expenditure
findings.detail: The council faces demand for 150 SEND specialist placements that are not available in-city, forcing it to place children in high-cost out-of-county provision. Capital projects are attempting to expand provision but the gap persists.
findings.matters: This represents an identified budget pressure where demand exceeds funded supply. High-cost out-of-county placements represent unbudgeted or under-budgeted spending pressure on revenue.
findings.figures: 150 placements required that are not available within city; current provision: 5 specialist settings, 9 enhanced resource provisions
findings.quote: Demand for specialist provision within Peterborough greatly outstrips places available. At the current time 150 placements are required that are not readily available within city, with a significant number of children attending high cost out of county placements as a result.

findings.paper_title: (a) Appendix F - PCC - Capital Strategy 2026-2029, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Population growth of 2% annually creating structural demand pressures on services
findings.detail: Peterborough is one of the fastest-growing cities in Britain with annual population growth of 2% and inward migration. This creates ongoing pressure for investment in schools, transport, and specialist provision that must be funded on top of existing commitments.
findings.matters: Growing councils typically have more demand for capital than static councils, and Peterborough's growth means ongoing capital pressure from new housing, schools, and infrastructure needs that may outpace grant funding.
findings.figures: Annual population growth approximately 2%
findings.quote: As a growing unitary authority in the heart of the East of England, Peterborough faces exciting opportunities alongside real pressures: annual population growth of around 2%, increasing demand for services, housing and infrastructure and the need to adapt to climate change.

findings.paper_title: (a) Appendix F - PCC - Capital Strategy 2026-2029, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Limited reserves and restricted revenue contribution to capital programme
findings.detail: The strategy acknowledges 'limited reserves' and states that Direct Revenue Financing amounts available for capital are 'unlikely to be material' given General Fund revenue pressures. This removes a traditional funding source for capital projects.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's cash buffers and flexibility. Limited reserves mean less ability to absorb unexpected costs or revenue shocks.
findings.figures: No specific reserve figures disclosed in this document; revenue contributions to capital described as 'unlikely to be material'
findings.quote: The Strategy recognises the financial challenges facing the Council, including inflationary pressures, limited reserves and the need to maintain a stable and sustainable revenue position.

findings.paper_title: (a) Appendix F - PCC - Capital Strategy 2026-2029, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Council explicitly states additional borrowing may not be prudent, affordable, or sustainable
findings.detail: Despite a £346m capital programme, the strategy warns that new borrowing is constrained by revenue pressures. The council is attempting to fund 71% of capital investment (£245m of £346m) from grants and third-party contributions, with remaining £101m from capital receipts and internal resources, treating borrowing as a 'last resort'.
findings.matters: This signals the council's own assessment that its debt capacity is limited and that future capital investment will depend heavily on external funding availability rather than borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £346m total capital programme; £245m grants/third-party (71%); £101m corporate resources; borrowing described as 'last resort'
findings.quote: Due to the existing pressures on the Council's revenue budget, additional borrowing may not be prudent, affordable, or sustainable. It is therefore essential, as far as possible, that all new capital expenditure is funded from Capital Grants, Capital Receipts, S106 / CIL and external / partnership funding, except where there is a strong business case to utilise borrowing facilities

findings.paper_title: (a) Appendix F - PCC - Capital Strategy 2026-2029, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement of £629m against realisable assets of only £482m
findings.detail: The council has borrowed historically for assets no longer on its balance sheet (academy school transfers) and non-realisable assets (roads and infrastructure). This creates a structural mismatch where the council's historic borrowing decisions cannot be recovered through asset sales.
findings.matters: This asymmetry limits the council's ability to reduce debt through asset disposals and suggests past borrowing decisions have reduced financial flexibility without corresponding asset retention.
findings.figures: CFR £629 million; realisable assets £482 million; difference of £147 million
findings.quote: The 2024/25 Statement of Accounts shows the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR), a measure of the capital expenditure incurred historically by the Council that has yet to be financed, the underlying need to borrow, at £629 million. Total realisable assets (property, plant and equipment & investment property) held by the Council are shown at £482 million.

findings.paper_title: (a) Appendix F - PCC - Capital Strategy 2026-2029, 10/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Existing debt burden of £507m with financing costs taking 17% of revenue budget
findings.detail: The council carries net borrowing of £507 million as of 31 March 2025, with annual borrowing costs consuming 17% of the 2024/25 revenue budget (expected to drop only to 16% in 2026/27). This represents a significant structural constraint on the council's revenue flexibility.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how much of the council's revenue stream is already committed to servicing existing debt, and how little room exists for new borrowing or revenue pressures.
findings.figures: £507 million net borrowing at 31/3/25; 17% of 2024/25 revenue budget; 16% expected 2026/27
findings.quote: Net borrowing at 31/3/25 was £507 million. The borrowing costs associated with that debt represent approximately 17% of the 2024/25 revenue budget.

findings.headline: NHS burden-shifting causing material pressure on adult and children's social care costs
findings.detail: The council identifies that 'Savings targets placed on the NHS are being indirectly passed to the council and the council inevitably has to pick up a greater proportion of health and social care costs'. Specifically visible in Continuing Health Care funding gaps for children in care. The council notes this 'is causing significant pressure for the Council and communication with the ICB on this matter is active'. This is a structural reallocation of cost from health to local government.
findings.matters: This is a funding shift outside the council's control. Unlike demand that can be managed, this is cost transfer from a better-funded body. It will persist and likely worsen.
findings.figures: Specific instance: Continuing Health Care funding gaps for children in care; described as causing 'significant pressure'
findings.quote: Savings targets placed on the NHS are being indirectly passed to the council and the council inevitably has to pick up a greater proportion of health and social care costs. The Council is specifically seeing this in instances where Continuing Health Care is applicable for Children in care. This is causing significant pressure for the Council

findings.headline: Entire 2026/27 budget balanced conditionally on exceptional government funding not yet confirmed
findings.detail: The budget is constructed on the assumption that two exceptional measures will be approved: a Flexible Use of Capital Receipts extension (£1.6m) and an Exceptional Financial Support capitalisation direction (£5.7m). The CFO states the council expects confirmation 'in early February' but 'at this stage the Council has not received confirmation this has been approved'. If either fails, 'the reserves position will be severely impacted and will not be sustainable for 2026/27'. The CFO explicitly flags that further discussion with MHCLG on emergency support would be needed.
findings.matters: The budget is contingent. If central government withholds funding that has not yet been formally approved, the council cannot balance without further emergency support or service reductions.
findings.figures: £1.6m flexible capital receipts (2026/27); £5.7m capitalisation direction (2026/27); total £7.3m of exceptional support built into balance
findings.quote: This view is reliant on the Flexible use of Capital Receipts Policy and the EFS request for a Capitalisation Direction being approved. Should these measures not be successful, the reserves position will be severely impacted and will not be sustainable for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation programme only funded for £0.1m of estimated £41m cost
findings.detail: Peterborough is preparing for local government reorganisation with new unitary authorities planned for 1 April 2028. The council estimates restructuring costs (closure, shadow authority, rebranding, ICT, redundancy, pension strain) at £41m across the region. The government provided £316k for the region (mostly spent on business cases). The council has set aside only £0.1m in reserves and £0.5m in capital budget for a £41m programme. Costs are 'expected to gradually ramp up by the end of the year with a full implementation programme being in place for 2027/28'.
