findings.matters: A £41m unfunded programme is being run from a council with critically low reserves. This will either force reserves depletion, force cuts to services, or require further emergency government support.
findings.figures: Option D business case: £41m one-off implementation cost across region; council allocation £0.1m reserves + £0.5m capital = £0.6m total
findings.quote: At present there is only £0.1m set aside as a specific commitment in the reserves, and £0.5m in the Capital Programme for associated ICT system and data costs.

findings.headline: DSG deficit forecast to reach £39.4m by March 2029; government takeover still uncertain
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant is running a growing deficit now at £12.5m and forecast to reach £39.4m by March 2029. The government plans to take over SEND funding from April 2028 but 'there is significant uncertainty around how the deficits accrued up to this date will be managed'. If left with the council, the new unitary authority will inherit a £38m+ liability. The council borrows to cover the deficit, costing £0.4m interest per £10m borrowed.
findings.matters: This is a £38m+ contingent liability hanging over the successor authority. If the government does not absorb it, it will either deplete reserves or trigger a capital financing charge that worsens the revenue budget.
findings.figures: DSG deficit at 31 March 2026 £12.5m; forecast 31 March 2029 £39.4m; interest cost approximately £0.4m per £10m borrowed
findings.quote: Should the Government leave these to be dealt with locally this will result in the new authority having to make good the forecast c£38m deficit, and a proportion of the deficit Cambridgeshire County Council is holding.

findings.headline: Children's exceptional high-cost placements running at over £100k per week
findings.detail: The council identifies exceptional high-cost placements as 'a real pressure' within the current year budgetary control report. One placement runs at 'over £100k per week', equating to £5.2m+ per year. Standard residential placements average £0.3m. The 2025/26 outturn is forecast at £7m overspend 'largely resulting from children's high cost placements'. This is a structural demand issue not being controlled.
findings.matters: This is unpredictable, volatile demand that the council has poor levers to control. It is eating the budget in real time and the council has no demonstrated containment strategy.
findings.figures: One exceptional placement at 'over £100k per week'; standard residential placements average £0.3m; 2025/26 forecast overspend £7m largely from this cause
findings.quote: The cost of an exceptionally high-cost placement at a run rate of over £100k per week. This has been a real pressure for the Council as reported within the current year Budgetary Control Report.

findings.headline: Previous £22m savings programme resulted in budgetary pressure; reset to modest £3.9m for 2026/27
findings.detail: The 2025/26 savings plan was £22m but 'a portion of these have resulted in budgetary pressure'. For 2026/27 the council has reset to a 'more achievable cashable savings target of £3.9m' plus £1.4m non-cashable. The document notes 'some risks linked to previous savings persist' but efforts are underway to mitigate by 2026/27. This is a dramatic downgrade signalling that planned savings have not materialised.
findings.matters: A council that cannot deliver savings is dependent on growth or reserves. Neither is available here. If the £3.9m reset target itself fails, the budget will not balance.
findings.figures: 2025/26 savings plan £22m; 2026/27 cashable savings target £3.9m; non-cashable savings £1.4m
findings.quote: The budget for 2025/26 features savings plans exceeding £22m, though a portion of these have resulted in budgetary pressure.

findings.headline: Borrowing £0.5bn with 16% of net revenue budget consumed by debt service
findings.detail: The council's overall borrowing stands at approximately £0.5bn. Capital financing costs alone consume 16% of the net revenue budget. The comparative benchmarking chart explicitly shows Peterborough's debt as a percentage of budget requirement is significantly higher than peer unitary authorities, whilst reserves are proportionally lower—a dangerous combination.
findings.matters: High leverage combined with weak reserves means the council has minimal buffer if interest rates rise on the £56m of maturing debt or if revenue conditions worsen. Refinancing risk is material.
findings.figures: £0.5bn total borrowing; £56m maturing in 2026/27 at average rate of 4.84%; capital financing 16% of net revenue budget
findings.quote: This council's overall borrowing remains high at c£0.5bn, with capital financing equating to approximately 16% of the net revenue budget.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves rated RED and described as 'incredibly low' until 2027/28
findings.detail: The CFO explicitly states reserves will fall to £22m by end March 2026 and remain critically inadequate. The sensitivity table shows total calculated risks exceed current General Fund balance. The CFO concludes reserves 'may not be sufficient to mitigate all risks, should they materialise' and warns that without exceptional government funding the position 'will not be sustainable for 2026/27'.
findings.matters: This is the core signal of financial distress. A council without reserves cannot absorb service demand spikes, lost income, or unexpected costs—exactly when those are most likely.
findings.figures: £22m forecast at 31 March 2026; General Fund balance £9.216m at 31 March 2026; Council characterises this as 'incredibly low financial resilience until 2027/28'
findings.quote: reserves balances projected as at 1 April 2026 remain low and may not be sufficient to mitigate all risks, should they materialise

findings.headline: Government's Fairer Funding Review has substantially improved Peterborough's settlement for three years
findings.detail: The confirmed Provisional Settlement in December 2025 provides significant funding improvements for 2026/27 through 2028/29, better reflecting local needs. This enables the council to present a balanced budget across the MTFS period and is the foundation for the council's financial strategy of rebuilding reserves and focusing on long-term sustainability.
findings.matters: A substantial, multi-year funding improvement is material to the council's ability to recover. However, this is dependent on government funding decisions remaining stable and the council's ability to deliver against plans.
findings.figures: Fairer Funding Review confirmed in December 2025 Provisional Settlement; enables balanced budget 2026/27–2028/29
findings.quote: the Government's Fairer Funding Review (FFR) was consulted on and confirmed in December 2025 within the multi‑year Provisional Settlement. This confirmed substantial improvements in funding for Peterborough over the next three years, better reflecting local needs and providing significantly enhanced financial stability.

findings.headline: Council Tax is being increased to the maximum referendum limit, leaving no headroom
findings.detail: The council is proposing a 4.99% council tax increase, which is at the maximum level before triggering a referendum. This suggests the council is using all available revenue-raising powers.
findings.matters: Maximising council tax signals limited other funding options and limited room to respond if budgets worsen. It also increases resident pressure on the council.
findings.figures: Proposed Council Tax increase of 4.99%
findings.quote: A proposed Council Tax increase of 4.99% in 2026/27.

findings.headline: SEND deficits are being funded through additional borrowing, straining the General Fund
findings.detail: The council faces persistent demand-driven pressure from SEND services, resulting in a Dedicated Schools Grant deficit. This is being funded through borrowing, which further increases the council's debt burden and the strain on the General Fund. While government has committed to fully funding SEND from April 2028, uncertainty remains about how existing deficits will be handled, creating risk of significant reserve depletion or additional borrowing.
findings.matters: Demand-driven deficits outside the council's control are creating structural borrowing. If not resolved as government intends, this could force large unexpected borrowing or reserve draws.
findings.figures: DSG increased by approximately £13.5m for 2026/27 (rising to £354.0m from £340.5m); High Needs Block increased £3.2m (5.82%)
findings.quote: The council continues to face major financial pressures due to increased demands on SEND services, leading to a DSG deficit. Funding the deficit requires borrowing, further straining the General Fund. Although a strategy is in place and the Government plans to fully fund SEND from April 2028, uncertainty remains over how existing deficits will be handled.

findings.headline: High debt levels of approximately £0.5bn with annual servicing costs of nearly £40m
findings.detail: The council carries substantial borrowing that consumes nearly £40m annually in debt servicing costs. This is a fixed cost that constrains the budget and limits the council's ability to respond to new pressures.
findings.matters: High debt servicing is a fixed charge on revenues. Combined with low reserves and uncertain savings, this creates significant refinancing and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Borrowing approximately £0.5bn; debt servicing costs nearly £40m annually
findings.quote: High debt levels: Borrowing stands at approximately £0.5bn, resulting in debt servicing costs of nearly £40m annually.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves are below the adequate level and will fall further
findings.detail: The CFO projects reserves of £9.2m at 1 April 2026, below the advised minimum of £11.7m (5% of net revenue expenditure). The Robustness Statement explicitly warns that reserves may not be sufficient to mitigate all risks and leave the council vulnerable to financial shocks.
findings.matters: Inadequate reserves limit the council's ability to absorb service pressures, demand spikes, or income shortfalls. This is a core measure of financial resilience.
findings.figures: Projected reserves £9.2m vs advised minimum £11.7m; advised minimum is 5% of NRE
findings.quote: the General Fund Reserve is expected to reduce to £9.2m at the end of 2025/26, below the advised level of £11.7m (5% of Net Revenue Expenditure). reserves remain low, leaving the council vulnerable to financial shocks.

findings.headline: Council has submitted an Exceptional Financial Support request to MHCLG to cover the shortfall
findings.detail: The council is requesting emergency government support to protect reserves. The CFO notes that even if approved, reserves will remain insufficient for the scale of financial risks the council faces.
findings.matters: The council cannot self-fund its position and is dependent on discretionary government support. This signals distress and limits flexibility.
findings.figures: EFS request submitted to MHCLG; approval uncertain
findings.quote: To protect these, a request for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) has been submitted to MHCLG. Even if approved, reserves will remain insufficient for an authority facing such inherent risks and substantial net expenditure.

findings.headline: A forecast £7m overspend in 2025/26 from savings that did not land
findings.detail: The council had a balanced budget for 2025/26, but high-risk savings and service pressures did not materialise as planned, creating a forecast overspend of £7m. This further strains reserves that are already depleted from prior-year pressures including transformation costs, children's services improvements, and inflation.
findings.matters: Shows planned cost reductions are not being delivered, a core risk for any borrower. The council cannot finance its operations as projected.
findings.figures: £7m overspend forecast in 2025/26
findings.quote: In 2025/26 the budget was balanced, but several high‑risk savings and service pressures have materialised, resulting in a forecast £7m overspend, putting further strain on already low reserves.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement reversal: debt burden projected to increase after 2027/28, ending the temporary period of debt reduction
findings.detail: The CFR falls from £626.6m (2025/26 est) to £619.1m (2026/27 est) and £611.6m (2027/28 est), but then rises to £614.2m (2028/29 est). This reversal is driven by the net financing requirement jumping to £23.5m (2028/29) versus £12.1m-£12.9m in prior years, while MRP (statutory debt repayment) only decreases to £20.9m. The debt reduction trajectory does not sustain.
findings.matters: The reversal signals the council's capital program is not temporary but elevated beyond 2027/28, or that current MRP provisions are insufficient to sustain debt reduction, with implications for long-term debt sustainability and future revenue budget pressure
findings.quote: Net financing requirement     23.5; Less MRP & Other financing  (20.9); CFR Carried Forward  614.2

findings.headline: Cash reserves are thin relative to capital spending: total treasury investments only £33.2m against planned annual capital programs of £75.9m-£113.2m
findings.detail: Section 12.1 states the council 'has run down its cash balances in recent years' due to internal borrowing strategy. As at 31 December 2025, total treasury investments (liquid reserves) were only £33.2m: £16m deposits with local authorities, £1.15m with banks, and £16.06m in money market funds. Annual capital spending is budgeted at £75.9m-£113.2m.
findings.matters: Thin cash reserves constrain the council's ability to absorb timing mismatches between capital expenditure and grant/revenue receipts, creating liquidity risk that becomes material when combined with grant dependency and planned capital intensity
findings.quote: Due to its internal borrowing position, the Council has run down its cash balances in recent years, however surplus cash will be generated from reserves and cash flow movements, e.g. grant/contributions received in advance of spend

findings.headline: Significant loan maturities over next 3 years require refinancing; council has flagged this as material refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council's debt maturity profile shows substantial amounts falling due for refinancing during 2026-2029. The 10+ year portion represents 65% of outstanding debt (£305.8m of £478.9m total), but significant maturities exist across all periods. Section 8.1 explicitly states: 'There are significant maturities over the next three financial years, and these maturities will need to be managed/refinanced carefully in order to reduce refinancing risk further.'
findings.matters: The council's current average borrowing cost is 3.92%, but maturing debt must be refinanced at future market rates. If rates remain elevated, refinancing costs will increase revenue financing charges materially, particularly given the council is betting on rates falling while facing large maturities
findings.figures: Total external borrowing: £478.9m at average 3.92%; 65% matures 10+ years out (£305.8m); 9% matures within 12 months (£43.2m)
findings.quote: There are significant maturities over the next three financial years, and these maturities will need to be managed/refinanced carefully in order to reduce refinancing risk further

findings.headline: Council delaying external borrowing, betting on PWLB rates falling; will only borrow at declining trigger rates of 4.50%, 4.25%, then 4.0%
findings.detail: Section 6.1 states the council is 'currently maintaining an internal borrowing position' and deferring external borrowing on the assumption long-term rates will fall. Trigger rates are set at 4.50% (current), 4.25% (2026/27), and 4.0% (2027/28). Section 5.5 notes 'caution will be adopted with the 2026/27 treasury operations' reflecting uncertainty about this rate outlook.
findings.matters: If PWLB rates remain elevated or rise contrary to forecast, the council will exhaust its limited cash reserves faster or be forced to borrow at unfavorable rates, creating material revenue pressure on future budgets with no stated contingency
findings.figures: Trigger rates: 4.50%, 4.25%, 4.0%; Bank Rate forecast 3.75% (Dec 2025) declining to 3.25% (Q4 2026); current PWLB Certainty Rate 'significantly above' the 3.25% neutral level
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an internal borrowing position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with external loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels

findings.headline: Council reserves depleting sharply: internal borrowing forecast to fall 56% from £90m to £40m over three years as capital programs consume cash
findings.detail: The council currently uses reserves and cash balances (internal borrowing) to fund capital needs. Internal borrowing is estimated at £90m (2025/26 est) and projected to decline to £60m (2026/27), £50m (2027/28), and £40m (2028/29). Section 4.4 explicitly states this capacity will fall as 'reserves, balances and grants, currently set aside, are utilised over the next three years to fund budgeted expenditure.'
findings.matters: Depleting reserves reduce financial flexibility and force the council into external borrowing at prevailing rates, increasing vulnerability to interest rate shocks and refinancing risk, particularly given significant debt maturities in the 2026-2029 period
findings.figures: Internal borrowing: £90.0m (2025/26 est), £60.0m (2026/27), £50.0m (2027/28), £40.0m (2028/29); decline of 56% over three years
findings.quote: the capacity to use internal borrowing is expected to fall as reserves, balances and grants, currently set aside, are utilised over the next three years to fund budgeted expenditure

findings.headline: Capital expenditure surges 49% to £113.2m in 2026/27, predominantly in Place & Economy, creating significant funding requirement
findings.detail: The council's capital program jumps from £75.9m (2025/26 est) to £113.2m (2026/27 est), with Place & Economy accounting for £71.9m. This is substantially above historical spend (£56.6m actual 2024/25) and drops back to £83.1m and £73.8m in following years. By the August 2026 document read date, this spending is already in flight.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this £113m program is fully funded, whether delivery is on track, and whether revenue implications are absorbed in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy without creating budget pressure
findings.figures: Capital expenditure 2026/27: £113.2m total, £71.9m Place & Economy, versus £56.6m actual 2024/25, £75.9m est 2025/26

findings.committee: Joint Meeting of the Scrutiny Committees
findings.headline: Investment income declining as Bank Rate cuts compress yields while cash balances shrink
findings.detail: Average investment returns are forecast to fall from current levels to 3.40% in 2026/27 and 3.30% thereafter, reflecting expected Bank Rate cuts. This decline in returns coincides with falling internal borrowing (and thus smaller cash balances available to invest), compressing the council's treasury contribution to the General Fund at a time when broader budget pressures appear to be forcing reserve drawdowns.
findings.matters: Declining investment income reduces a source of budget flexibility. Combined with reserve depletion to fund operations, it tightens the council's overall financial headroom.
findings.figures: Forecast investment returns 3.40% (2026/27), 3.30% (2027/28–29); current cash as at Dec-25 £33.2m
findings.quote: Investment returns are expected to fall further throughout 2026/27. MUFG are currently forecasting bank rate to reduce to 3.25% by the end of 2026

findings.committee: Joint Meeting of the Scrutiny Committees
findings.headline: Borrowing strategy depends on forecast fall in long-term interest rates; risks if forecast does not materialise
findings.detail: The council is deferring new external borrowing, maintaining internal borrowing instead, on the basis that PWLB long-term rates are 'expected to fall from their current levels' once inflation concerns ease. MUFG forecasts Bank Rate to fall from current 3.75% to 3.25% by end-2026. However, the paper acknowledges 'risks to the forecasts to the upside, especially if inflation remains higher than expected and risk premiums relating to government debt increase'.
findings.matters: If long-term rates do not fall as forecast—or if they rise further due to inflation surprises or fiscal/geopolitical shocks—the council faces a strategic mismatch: depleting reserves while rates remain elevated could force expensive external borrowing at precisely the wrong time in the cycle.
findings.figures: Trigger rates for new borrowing: 4.50% (current), 4.25% (2026/27), 4.0% (2027/28); PWLB certainty rate currently gilts + 80 bps
findings.quote: This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels, albeit only once prevailing inflation concerns are addressed by restrictive near-term monetary policy

findings.committee: Joint Meeting of the Scrutiny Committees
findings.headline: Significant debt maturities over next three years requiring refinancing in a concentrated long-dated debt portfolio
findings.detail: As at 31 December 2025, 63% of outstanding debt (£305.8m) matures in 10+ years, creating a structured refinancing wave. The paper explicitly flags that 'significant maturities over the next three financial years' must be 'managed/refinanced carefully' to reduce refinancing risk—implying tighter control will be needed if interest rates remain elevated.
findings.matters: If refinancing requirements coincide with sustained high borrowing rates, the council faces elevated cost of debt service. This risk is compounded by depleting reserves reducing the council's ability to defer refinancing if rates are unfavourable.
findings.figures: £305.8m (63% of debt) in 10+ year maturity band; as at Dec-25, external borrowing £478.9m; PWLB debt £458.9m at avg 3.91%
findings.quote: There are significant maturities over the next three financial years, and these maturities will need to be managed/refinanced carefully in order to reduce refinancing risk further

findings.committee: Joint Meeting of the Scrutiny Committees
findings.headline: Internal borrowing (reserves) declining from £90m to £40m over three years
findings.detail: The council maintains an internal borrowing position (using cash and reserves rather than external debt), but this capacity is explicitly forecast to fall sharply—from £90m in 2025/26 to £60m in 2026/27 and £40m by 2028/29. The council acknowledges it is using up reserves and grant advances to fund budgeted expenditure as external borrowing requires external debt repayment at higher current rates.
findings.matters: A £50m reduction in internal resources over three years materially weakens the council's financial flexibility and liquidity cushion, particularly if unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls arise.
findings.quote: the capacity to use internal borrowing is expected to fall as reserves, balances and grants, currently set aside, are utilised over the next three years to fund budgeted expenditure

findings.headline: Notable refinancing risk: £57.0m of debt concentrated in 12-24 month maturity band
findings.detail: Of the council's £488.8m external borrowing, £57.0m (12%) matures in 12-24 months, creating a notable concentration in near-term refinancing needs. While the council has a mitigation strategy in place and 66% of debt is long-dated, the near-term maturity concentration exposes the council to refinancing risk if credit spreads widen or market conditions tighten.
findings.matters: Concentrated debt maturities create timing risk; if credit markets tighten or spreads widen, the council could face materially higher borrowing costs when rolling over £57m of debt
findings.figures: £57.0m maturing in 12-24 months; £488.8m total external borrowing; 12% of borrowing in 12-24 month band
findings.quote: there is a notable re-financing risk in maturities anticipated in 1 to 2 years range. To reduce re-financing risk and improve liquidity management, future borrowing activity will be focused on smoothing the maturity profile.

findings.headline: Capital financing budget pressure of £2.2m from Estimated Credit Loss on Hilton Hotel loan
findings.detail: The council has recognised an Estimated Credit Loss on the Hilton Hotel loan, triggering a £2.2m accounting provision that increased capital financing budget pressure between Q1 and Q2. This indicates deterioration in the performance or credit quality of this capital investment, with the impact now flowing through to reduce the council's revenue budget flexibility.
findings.matters: Credit losses on council lending signal underperformance of capital investments and reduce available resources for other priorities; indicates investment or lending risk embedded in the balance sheet
findings.figures: £2.2m capital financing budget pressure
findings.quote: That change between quarter 1 and quarter 2 is due to the required accounting treatment to reflect the Estimated Credit Loss (ECL) in respect of the Hilton Hotel loan. This pressure has had an impact on this ratio, as the costs taken on a greater proportion of the Councils budget.

findings.paper_title: Item 07. PCC Audit Results Report - 13 November 2025
findings.headline: Auditor warns of potential Statutory Recommendations if improvements not made in 2025/26
findings.detail: The auditor has not issued a Statutory Recommendation (a formal public report under Schedule 7 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act) at this point, but warns: 'However, if we are not satisfied with the pace and substance of improvements in addressing our Recommendation 1 (Page 47) as part of the 2025/26 audit, we would be minded to issue Statutory Recommendations at that point, given the recurring inability to prepare robust financial statements and support the audit process.'
findings.matters: Statutory Recommendations are a serious escalation that signals public auditor concern about governance and financial management. If issued, they would be formally reported to the Secretary of State.
findings.figures: No Statutory Recommendations at present; warning of potential future issue
findings.quote: However, if we are not satisfied with the pace and substance of improvements in addressing our Recommendation 1 (Page 47) as part of the 2025/26 audit, we would be minded to issue Statutory Recommendations at that point, given the recurring inability to prepare robust financial statements and support the audit process.

findings.paper_title: Item 07. PCC Audit Results Report - 13 November 2025
findings.headline: Auditor cannot complete Minimum Revenue Provision (debt repayment) audit due to late council response
findings.detail: The council did not respond to audit queries on MRP (Minimum Revenue Provision—the amount set aside to repay borrowing) in a timely manner. The auditor used up their allocated audit window waiting for the response, meaning MRP audit procedures could not be completed. The council set aside £18.9 million MRP in 2024/25.
findings.matters: MRP determines how much of the council's revenue is committed to debt repayment. If not properly calculated, the council may underfund debt repayment or overfund it, affecting financial stability.
findings.figures: £18.9 million Minimum Revenue Provision set aside in 2024/25
findings.quote: The Council did not respond to our follow up queries in a timely manner, finally providing a response after we had utilised our allocated audit window. Whilst we have gained some assurance from our procedures, we have not ben able to complete all procedures and are therefore unable to conclude our work in relation to Minimum Revenue Provision.

findings.paper_title: Item 07. PCC Audit Results Report - 13 November 2025
findings.headline: Auditor unable to complete audit of IFRS 16 leases implementation
findings.detail: IFRS 16 (leases accounting standard) became mandatory for local government in 2024/25. The council did not complete its analysis of IFRS 16 impact and did not implement the standard in the 2024/25 financial statements. The auditor was therefore unable to audit this area, and this limitation contributed to the disclaimer of opinion.
findings.matters: IFRS 16 requires recognition of right-of-use assets and lease liabilities on the balance sheet. Failure to implement it means the council's lease obligations are not disclosed, potentially understating liabilities.
findings.figures: IFRS 16 leases not auditable; implementation not completed
findings.quote: The 2024/25 draft financial statements did not account for the implementation of IFRS 16 as the Council had not completed their analysis of the leases/assets caught within this revised accounting standard. We were therefore unable to audit the implementation of IFRS 16... this limitation has contributed to our consideration that will lead to a disclaimer of the 2024/25 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Item 07. PCC Audit Results Report - 13 November 2025
findings.headline: £1.7 million payroll PAYE/NI unreconciled to general ledger after system migration
findings.detail: The council changed payroll systems during 2024/25. As of 31 March 2025, the council had not reconciled £1.7 million of PAYE/National Insurance and £1.1 million of pension contributions between the payroll system and the general ledger. The council could not provide working papers to demonstrate the data migration was complete and accurate.
findings.matters: Unreconciled payroll amounts totalling £2.8 million suggest the payroll system migration was not properly controlled or verified. This is a critical operational system for any organization.
findings.figures: £1.7 million PAYE/National Insurance unreconciled; £1.1 million pension contributions unreconciled
findings.quote: The Council were unable to provide any supporting working papers to demonstrate that the data migration from ResourceLink and Unit 4 HRP was complete and accurate... The Council does not perform reconciliations between the Payroll system and the General Ledger for Council payroll. As part of our audit procedures, we identified £1.7 million of PAYE/National Insurance and £1.1 million of Pension Contributions which remained unreconciled as of 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Item 07. PCC Audit Results Report - 13 November 2025
findings.headline: No formal controls over journal authorisation before posting to general ledger
findings.detail: The auditor identified that the council has no formal procedure for authorizing manual journals before they are posted to the general ledger. This is a significant control weakness that creates fraud risk and was identified as a recurring issue the auditor 'wanted to bring to the attention of the Audit Committee.'
findings.matters: Lack of journal authorization controls is a critical internal control failure. It creates material fraud risk and suggests the council cannot prevent unauthorized or erroneous transactions entering the accounts.
findings.figures: Manual journals without authorization detected during audit
findings.quote: Our audit procedures identified that the Council does not have any formal procedure in place for the authorisation of journals before they are posted to the General Ledger. Whilst we have raised this as a control weakness, we have not currently identified any instances where this has led to management override.

findings.paper_title: Item 07. PCC Audit Results Report - 13 November 2025
findings.headline: £18.5 million overstatement in investment in university company subsidiary
findings.detail: The council's investment in Peterborough HE Property Company Limited was overstated by £18.530 million. The university building became operational in 2024/25, reducing the subsidiary's net worth, but the council did not adjust its investment valuation downward to reflect the subsidiary's true value.
findings.matters: This shows the council is not properly valuing its major investments and does not have adequate processes to track changes in subsidiary performance.
findings.figures: £18.530 million overstatement
findings.quote: Our audit procedures identified an overstatement of £18.530 million in Long-Term Investments. This misstatement is in relation to the Council's investment in Peterborough HE Property Company Limited. The valuation of the subsidiary entity has reduced due to the related Peterborough University building becoming operational in 2024/25, thereby reducing the net worth of Peterborough HE Property Company Limited.

findings.paper_title: Item 07. PCC Audit Results Report - 13 November 2025
findings.headline: £199 million pension liability misstatement due to accounting error
findings.detail: The auditor identified a £199.051 million error in the pension liability valuation due to the council incorrectly applying asset ceiling methodology. While this was corrected in the financial statements, it represents a fundamental accounting error on one of the council's largest liabilities.
findings.matters: A large accounting error on pension liabilities, even if caught and corrected, signals weak financial controls and raises questions about what else might be wrong.
findings.figures: £199.051 million audit difference; pension asset/liability balance sheet position £179 million (assets £725m, liabilities £546m)
findings.quote: Our audit procedures identified an audit differences of £199.051 million in relation to an increase in the valuation of Pension Liability. The misstatement was due to the impact of the asset ceiling on the valuation of the Pension Liability.

findings.paper_title: Item 07. PCC Audit Results Report - 13 November 2025
findings.headline: Auditor cannot verify £23 million solar panel asset portfolio valuation
findings.detail: The council owns approximately 7,700 solar panels from a £23 million deal in 2021, valued using a complex specialist model developed in 2020/21. The council did not update the model for inclusion in the 2024/25 financial statements, meaning the auditor cannot verify the valuation or its reasonableness. This is a significant asset that cannot be audited.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assess whether this major asset is correctly valued. If the model is wrong, the asset could be overstated by material amounts, affecting the balance sheet.
findings.figures: £23 million solar panel portfolio; approximately 7,700 solar panels
findings.quote: The Council did not update the Solar Panel Asset Portfolio model for inclusion within the 2024/25 financial statements. We were therefore unable to audit the valuation of these assets. We are therefore unable to gain assurance over the valuation of the Solar Panel Asset Portfolio, and this limitation has contributed to our consideration that will lead to a disclaimer of the 2024/25 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Item 07. PCC Audit Results Report - 13 November 2025
findings.headline: £10.5 million impairment on Hilton Hotel regeneration loan after company administration
findings.detail: The council made a £15 million loan to Fletton Quays Hotel Ltd for the Hilton Hotel. The construction company went into administration on 17 October 2023. A proposed sale in October 2024 did not complete, and as of 31 March 2025 the building remains with the Administrators. The council has now impaired the loan by £10.5 million, reducing the carrying value from £14.8 million to £4.3 million.
findings.matters: This is a major capital project failure resulting in a £10.5 million loss. A lender needs to know the council has lost capital on a regeneration scheme and that the asset remains in administrator hands with no resolution in sight.
findings.figures: £15 million original loan facility; £10.5 million impairment; £4.3 million remaining valuation
findings.quote: The company responsible for the construction of the Fletton Quays Hilton Hotel was put into administration by the Council on 17 October 2023... In October 2024, the Council's Cabinet approved the transfer of the hotel from the Administrators to a preferred bidder. However, the proposed sale did not subsequently complete. The building is still with the Administrators as of 2024/25 financial year... Management's Expected Credit Loss Assessment concluded that the loan should be impaired by £10.5 million, as the current value of the part completed hotel asset or its future economic benefit is only valued at £4.3 million at the 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Item 07. PCC Audit Results Report - 13 November 2025
findings.headline: Fourth consecutive year of audit disclaimer on financial statements
findings.detail: The auditor will issue a disclaimer of opinion on the 2024/25 statements, continuing a pattern from 2021/22, 2022/23, and 2023/24. The auditor lacks sufficient evidence over opening balances, in-year movements, and closing balances, meaning financial position cannot be verified. A disclaimer signals the financial statements cannot be relied upon for decision-making.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assess financial health or credit risk when audited accounts carry a disclaimer. This is a fundamental credibility failure that affects every borrowing decision.
findings.figures: Disclaimers issued for 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, and anticipated for 2024/25
findings.quote: As a result of the disclaimer of opinion on the 2021/22, 2022,23, and 2023/24 financial statements, we do not have assurance over the brought forward balances from 2023/24 (the opening balances). This means we do not have assurance over all 2024/25 in-year movements and the comparative prior year movements... we are unable to conclude that the 2024/25 financial statements are free from material and pervasive misstatement. We therefore anticipate issuing a disclaimed 2024/25 audit opinion.
